17. INTRAUTERINE CONTRACEPTION

IUC methods are long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC) with licensed durations of use ranging between 3 and 10 years.

The LNG-IUS is a T-shaped device with an elastomers core containing levonorgestrel (LNG).

The 52 mg LNG-IUS (Mirena) releases approximately 20 µg LNG per day, reducing to approximately 10 µg per day after 5 years.

The 13.5 mg LNG-IUS (Jaydess) is licensed for contraception and has a release rate of approximately 14 µg per day for the first 24 days, decreasing to 5 µg per day after 3 years.

Mode of Action:

Both pre- and post-fertilization effects, interfere with implantation, reduced rates of blastocyst formation.

Cu-IUD is effective immediately following insertion. If fertilization has already occurred, the endometrial inflammatory reaction has been shown to have an anti-implantation effect.

Contraceptive Efficacy and Duration of Use: Women advised of the very low failure rates.
The most effective methods of IUC are the LNG-IUS methods and T-shaped devices with at least 380 mm² copper and copper bands on the transverse arms.

Criteria for excluding pregnancy She has not had intercourse since last normal menses

She has been correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception

She is within the first 7 days of the onset of a normal menstrual period

She is not breastfeeding and less than 4 weeks from giving birth

She is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic, and less than 6 months’ postpartum

She is within the first 7 days post-abortion or miscarriage

A negative pregnancy test, if available, adds weight to the exclusion of pregnancy, but only if ≥3 weeks since the last episode of unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI).

NB: In addition to the conditions mentioned above, health professionals should also consider whether a woman is at risk of becoming pregnant as a result of UPSI within the last 7 days.

 

Assessment before IUCD insertion:

Clinical assessment: detail history, UKMEC assessment before insertion.

STI risk assessment: A sexual history must be taken in order to identify women at risk of STI. Risk factors include:

Being sexually active and aged <25 years

Having a new sexual partner in the last 3 months

Having more than one sexual partner in the last year

Having a regular sexual partner who has other sexual partners

A history of STI and Alcohol/substance abuse

Attending as a previous contact of STI

Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely required for the insertion or removal of IUC, even in women with conditions where the risk of infective endocarditis may be increased.

Non Contraceptive:

Benefits of Mirena:

Endometrial and other cancer protection

Dysmenorrhea/pelvic pain: primary dysmenorrhea, endometriosis or adenomyosis

Heavy menstrual bleeding: The 52 mg LNG-IUS is effective in reducing menstrual blood loss and can be used in the management of HMB.

Hormonal side effects:

Weight: Weight gain has been observed with use of IUC. There is no significant difference between hormonal & non-hormonal intrauterine methods and evidence to support a causal association is lacking.

Health concerns/risks:

Irregular Bleeding: In the 3–6 months following IUC insertion, women may experience irregular, prolonged or frequent bleeding, but menstrual bleeding patterns tend to improve with time.

Breast cancer: Evidence does not support a link between breast cancer and use of LNG-IUS. Non-hormonal contraception is most appropriate for women with a history of breast cancer.

Cardiovascular health: Evidence suggests there is little or no increased risk of VTE or MI associated with the use of a LNG-IUS.

Ectopic pregnancy: If pregnancy does occur with an intrauterine method in situ, the risk of an ectopic pregnancy occurring is increased.

➤ Expulsion:

The risk of expulsion with IUC is around 1 in 20 and is most common in the first year of use, particularly within 3 months of insertion.

➤ post-abortion insertion:

There is no need to delay insertion of an IUC post-abortion providing woman has been informed of the small increased risk of expulsion.

➤ Ovarian cysts:

Although ovarian cysts may occur when using the LNG-IUS, most cysts are asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously.

➤ Vulvovaginal candida and bacterial vaginosis:

Cu-IUD users with recurrent BV or VVC may wish to consider an alternative method of contraception.

➤ Valid consent:

Valid consent should be given by women prior to both pelvic examination and IUC insertion or removal.

When inserting IUC, regardless of the setting, remember the following points:

Establish whether a reliable method of contraception was used before insertion and whether pregnancy can be excluded (see Box 1).

Obtain consent (written or verbal), including a description of the insertion procedure and the risks associated with it (failure rate, infection, expulsion and perforation).

Keep written documentation, including findings of bimanual and speculum examination.

Provide post-insertion information, including what to expect in terms of pain and bleeding and which symptoms should prompt urgent medical advice.

 

 

➤ Local anesthetic:

There is no evidence from current trials to support the use of topical lidocaine, misoprostol or NSAIDs for improving ease of insertion or reducing pain during insertion of intrauterine methods.

➤ post-procedure analgesia:

NSAIDs can be offered to women who experience pain after insertion of an intrauterine method. A bimanual pelvic examination should be performed on all women before inserting IUD.

➤ Managing Problems Associated with IUD:

✅ Unscheduled bleeding: For women with unscheduled bleeding who wish to continue with the LNG-IUS and are medically eligible,
a COC could be tried for up to 3 months.
NSAIDs can be considered in the management of problematic bleeding with use of Cu-IUDs.

➤ Managing Problems Associated with IUC:

Presence of actinomyces-like organisms (ALO):
Insertion or reinsertion of an intrauterine method can be carried out in asymptomatic women with ALOs.
There is no need to remove IUC in asymptomatic women with ALOs.

Suspected pelvic infection: IUD removal is not routinely required in women with PID but it should be removed if there is no response to treatment (approximately 72 hours)

Symptoms requiring medical attention: Women should be advised to seek medical assistance at any time if they develop symptoms of pelvic infection, pain, abnormal bleeding, late menstrual period (IUD), non-palpable threads or can feel the stem of the IUC.

Routine follow-up: A routine follow-up visit can be advised after the first menses following insertion of IUC or 3-6 weeks later.

For women with cardiac disease the decision to use IUD should involve a cardiologist. The IUD should be fitted in a hospital setting if a vasovagal reaction presents a particularly high risk, for example, women with single ventricle circulation, Eisenmenger physiology, tachycardia or pre-existing bradycardia.

Non-visible threads:

Step 1: Exclude pregnancy

Step 2: If not pregnant, advise alternative contraception and arrange ultrasound scan to locate the device

Step 3: If device located in uterus, assess for:

Leave in situ until due for removal, OR

Attempt removal with appropriate tools, OR

Refer for hysteroscopy if needed

If device not located:

Request X-ray of abdomen and pelvis.

If device located on X-ray, assess for perforation and manage accordingly.

Key Guidelines for Timing of IUD Removal/Replacement:

IUCD (Copper IUD):

Over 50 years of age: Remove 1 year after last menstrual period.

Under 50 years of age: Remove 2 years after last menstrual period.

LNG-IUS (Hormonal IUS):

If inserted at age 45 or above, it can be used for 7 years (instead of replacing at standard 5 years).

For planned pregnancy: Remove after pregnancy advice and lifestyle counseling.

When removed within licensed duration to switch methods: Ensure appropriate timing based on menstrual cycle.

If outside licensed duration:

Cu – IUD 380mm2 copper inserted > age 40 can be retained until menopause.

Replacement rules depend on age timing of last menstrual period.

Use of backup contraception or timing of reinsertion may be recommended depending on individual circumstances.
